claim: MprF is an enzyme that alters membrane compositions through covalent lipid modification.
source: One enzyme that alters membrane compositions through covalent lipid modification is MprF.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of MprF.

claim: Streptococcus agalactiae MprF synthesizes lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG) from anionic PG.
source: We recently identified that Streptococcus agalactiae MprF synthesizes lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG) from anionic PG, and a novel cationic lipid, lysyl-glucosyl-diacylglycerol (Lys-Glc-DAG), from neutral glycolipid Glc-DAG.
evidence: This is a recent finding by the authors as stated in the abstract.

claim: Streptococcus agalactiae MprF synthesizes lysyl-glucosyl-diacylglycerol (Lys-Glc-DAG) from neutral glycolipid Glc-DAG.
source: We recently identified that Streptococcus agalactiae MprF synthesizes lysyl-phosphatidylglycerol (Lys-PG) from anionic PG, and a novel cationic lipid, lysyl-glucosyl-diacylglycerol (Lys-Glc-DAG), from neutral glycolipid Glc-DAG.
evidence: This is a recent finding by the authors as stated in the abstract.

claim: A restricted Boltzmann machine-guided approach led to the discovery of diglucosyl-diacylglycerol (Glc2-DAG) as a new substrate for MprF in Enterococcus.
source: Second, a restricted Boltzmann machine-guided approach led us to discover an entirely new substrate for MprF in Enterococcus, diglucosyl-diacylglycerol (Glc2-DAG), and an expanded set of organisms that modify glycolipid substrates using MprF.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Lipids are critical for fundamental biological processes including the formation of cell membranes, protection, and cargo delivery; energy storage; and cell signaling pathways.
source: Lipids are ubiquitous and diverse group of amphiphathic compounds that are critical for fundamental biological processes, including the formation of cell membranes, protection, and cargo delivery; energy storage; and cell signaling pathways (Fahy et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fahy et al., 2011.

claim: Chemical modifications to lipids impact interactions and the physicochemical properties of membranes.
source: Chemical modifications to lipids, including changes in fatty acid tails (saturated and unsaturated) (Wang et al., 2018), modifications of head groups (Roy et al., 2009), and alterations to lipid charge (Roy and Ibba, 2008), impact these interactions, as well as the physicochemical properties of membranes.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Wang et al., 2018; Roy et al., 2009; Roy and Ibba, 2008).

claim: Bacteria commonly synthesize lipids that are negatively charged or neutral.
source: Commonly, bacteria synthesize lipids that are negatively charged or neutral (Sohlenkamp and Geiger, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sohlenkamp and Geiger, 2016.

claim: Some bacteria modify negatively charged lipids with amino acids to make them positively charged to confer resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides and cationic antibiotics.
source: Some bacteria modify the negatively charged lipids with amino acids to make them positively charged to confer resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides and cationic antibiotics (Weidenmaier et al., 2005; Joyce and Doran, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weidenmaier et al., 2005 and Joyce and Doran, 2023.

claim: Outer membrane vesicles containing modified lipopolysaccharide can be used to deliver siRNA to targeted cancer cells.
source: A study by Gujrati et al., 2014, used low cytotoxic outer membrane vesicles that contained a modified lipopolysaccharide to deliver siRNA to targeted cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gujrati et al., 2014.

claim: MprF modifies lipids through the transfer of amino acids from charged tRNAs to the head group of the anionic membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylglycerol (PG).
source: MprF modifies lipids through the transfer of amino acids from charged tRNAs to the head group of the anionic membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylglycerol (PG) (Roy and Ibba, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roy and Ibba, 2008.

claim: The MprF protein is comprised of an N-terminal flippase domain and a C-terminal synthase domain.
source: The MprF protein is comprised of two domains: an N-terminal flippase domain responsible for moving aminoacylated lipids from the inner membrane leaflet to the outer leaflet and a C-terminal synthase domain responsible for the aminoacyl transfer from tRNA to lipids (Ernst et al., 2009; Staubitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ernst et al., 2009 and Staubitz et al., 2004.

claim: The N-terminal flippase domain of MprF is responsible for moving aminoacylated lipids from the inner membrane leaflet to the outer leaflet.
source: The MprF protein is comprised of two domains: an N-terminal flippase domain responsible for moving aminoacylated lipids from the inner membrane leaflet to the outer leaflet and a C-terminal synthase domain responsible for the aminoacyl transfer from tRNA to lipids (Ernst et al., 2009; Staubitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ernst et al., 2009 and Staubitz et al., 2004.

claim: The C-terminal synthase domain of MprF is responsible for the aminoacyl transfer from tRNA to lipids.
source: The MprF protein is comprised of two domains: an N-terminal flippase domain responsible for moving aminoacylated lipids from the inner membrane leaflet to the outer leaflet and a C-terminal synthase domain responsible for the aminoacyl transfer from tRNA to lipids (Ernst et al., 2009; Staubitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ernst et al., 2009 and Staubitz et al., 2004.

claim: An S. agalactiae mprF deletion mutant no longer synthesizes Lys-Glc-DAG or Lys-PG.
source: An S. agalactiae mprF deletion mutant no longer synthesizes Lys-Glc-DAG or Lys-PG and expression of S. agalactiae mprF in the heterologous host Streptococcus mitis conferred Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG synthesis to S. mitis (Joyce et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Joyce et al., 2022.

claim: Expression of S. agalactiae mprF in the heterologous host Streptococcus mitis conferred Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG synthesis to S. mitis.
source: An S. agalactiae mprF deletion mutant no longer synthesizes Lys-Glc-DAG or Lys-PG and expression of S. agalactiae mprF in the heterologous host Streptococcus mitis conferred Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG synthesis to S. mitis (Joyce et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Joyce et al., 2022.

claim: MprF adding lysine onto a neutral glycolipid (Glc-DAG) was demonstrated for the first time in S. agalactiae.
source: This was the first time MprF was demonstrated to add lysine onto a neutral glycolipid (Glc-DAG).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the introduction.

claim: Streptococcus sobrinus ATCC 27352 MprF has 61.4% amino acid identity to S. agalactiae MprF.
source: A BLASTp analysis found that Streptococcus sobrinus ATCC 27352 MprF (WP_019790557.1) had 61.4% amino acid identity to the S. agalactiae MprF, Streptococcus salivarius ATCC 7073 MprF (WP_002888893.1) had 43.09% amino acid identity, Streptococcus ferus MprF (WP_018030543.1) had 61.88% amino acid identity, and Streptococcus downei (WP_002997695.1) had 61.03% amino acid identity (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on BLASTp analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Streptococcus salivarius ATCC 7073 MprF has 43.09% amino acid identity to S. agalactiae MprF.
source: A BLASTp analysis found that Streptococcus sobrinus ATCC 27352 MprF (WP_019790557.1) had 61.4% amino acid identity to the S. agalactiae MprF, Streptococcus salivarius ATCC 7073 MprF (WP_002888893.1) had 43.09% amino acid identity, Streptococcus ferus MprF (WP_018030543.1) had 61.88% amino acid identity, and Streptococcus downei (WP_002997695.1) had 61.03% amino acid identity (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on BLASTp analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Streptococcus ferus MprF has 61.88% amino acid identity to S. agalactiae MprF.
source: A BLASTp analysis found that Streptococcus sobrinus ATCC 27352 MprF (WP_019790557.1) had 61.4% amino acid identity to the S. agalactiae MprF, Streptococcus salivarius ATCC 7073 MprF (WP_002888893.1) had 43.09% amino acid identity, Streptococcus ferus MprF (WP_018030543.1) had 61.88% amino acid identity, and Streptococcus downei (WP_002997695.1) had 61.03% amino acid identity (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on BLASTp analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Streptococcus downei MprF has 61.03% amino acid identity to S. agalactiae MprF.
source: A BLASTp analysis found that Streptococcus sobrinus ATCC 27352 MprF (WP_019790557.1) had 61.4% amino acid identity to the S. agalactiae MprF, Streptococcus salivarius ATCC 7073 MprF (WP_002888893.1) had 43.09% amino acid identity, Streptococcus ferus MprF (WP_018030543.1) had 61.88% amino acid identity, and Streptococcus downei (WP_002997695.1) had 61.03% amino acid identity (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on BLASTp analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: S. mitis does not natively encode mprF.
source: S. mitis does not natively encode mprF but synthesizes lipids (Glc-DAG; PG) that are substrates for S. agalactiae MprF (Adams et al., 2017; Joyce et al., 2019; Joyce et al., 2022), making it an appropriate heterologous host for expressing streptococcal MprFs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adams et al., 2017; Joyce et al., 2019; Joyce et al., 2022.

claim: S. mitis synthesizes lipids (Glc-DAG; PG) that are substrates for S. agalactiae MprF.
source: S. mitis does not natively encode mprF but synthesizes lipids (Glc-DAG; PG) that are substrates for S. agalactiae MprF (Adams et al., 2017; Joyce et al., 2019; Joyce et al., 2022), making it an appropriate heterologous host for expressing streptococcal MprFs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adams et al., 2017; Joyce et al., 2019; Joyce et al., 2022.

claim: S. mitis NCTC12261 with empty vector control (pABG5) lacks lysine lipids.
source: (a) S. mitis NCTC12261 with empty vector control (pABG5) lacks lysine lipids
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a with lipidomic data.

claim: S. agalactiae mprF (pGBSMprF) produces both Lys-PG and Lys-Glc-DAG when expressed in S. mitis.
source: (b) S. agalactiae mprF (pGBSMprF) produces both Lys-PG and Lys-Glc-DAG
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b with lipidomic data.

claim: S. salivarius mprF produces only Lys-PG when expressed in S. mitis.
source: (c) S. salivarius mprF produces only Lys-PG
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c with lipidomic data.

claim: S. ferus mprF produces only Lys-Glc-DAG when expressed in S. mitis.
source: (d) S. ferus mprF produces only Lys-Glc-DAG.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2d with lipidomic data.

claim: S. sobrinus MprF confers synthesis of Lys-Glc-DAG, but not Lys-PG in S. mitis.
source: Lipidomic analysis found that pSobrinus, pDownei, and pFerus conferred synthesis of Lys-Glc-DAG, but not Lys-PG in S. mitis.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: S. downei MprF confers synthesis of Lys-Glc-DAG, but not Lys-PG in S. mitis.
source: Lipidomic analysis found that pSobrinus, pDownei, and pFerus conferred synthesis of Lys-Glc-DAG, but not Lys-PG in S. mitis.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: S. ferus MprF confers synthesis of Lys-Glc-DAG at a similar level to S. agalactiae MprF.
source: Notably, pFerus confers synthesis of Lys-Glc-DAG at a similar level to S. agalactiae MprF (Figure 2b and d).
evidence: This is based on comparison of lipidomic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: S. salivarius MprF synthesized Lys-PG at a level most similar to S. agalactiae MprF.
source: Importantly, S. salivarius MprF also synthesized Lys-PG at a level most similar to S. agalactiae MprF (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is based on comparison of lipidomic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Streptococcal MprF enzymes with higher amino acid percent (>60%) to S. agalactiae MprF conferred Lys-Glc-DAG synthesis to S. mitis.
source: In general, streptococcal MprF enzymes with higher amino acid percent (>60%) to S. agalactiae MprF conferred Lys-Glc-DAG synthesis to S. mitis, but only S. agalactiae MprF conferred both Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG synthesis in S. mitis.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the experimental results presented.

claim: Only S. agalactiae MprF conferred both Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG synthesis in S. mitis.
source: In general, streptococcal MprF enzymes with higher amino acid percent (>60%) to S. agalactiae MprF conferred Lys-Glc-DAG synthesis to S. mitis, but only S. agalactiae MprF conferred both Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG synthesis in S. mitis.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results presented.

claim: The Boltzmann machine formulation is closely related to the Potts model from physics.
source: The Boltzmann machine formulation is closely related to the Potts model from physics, which was successfully applied in biology to elucidate important residues in protein structure and function (Morcos et al., 2011), one example being the careful tuning of enzyme specificity in bacterial two-component regulatory systems (Cheng et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morcos et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2021.

claim: The Potts model was successfully applied in biology to elucidate important residues in protein structure and function.
source: The Boltzmann machine formulation is closely related to the Potts model from physics, which was successfully applied in biology to elucidate important residues in protein structure and function (Morcos et al., 2011), one example being the careful tuning of enzyme specificity in bacterial two-component regulatory systems (Cheng et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morcos et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2021.

claim: S. agalactiae MprF and other MprF enzymes that utilize glycolipid substrates have unique patterns of interacting residues relative to those enzymes that use only PG as a substrate.
source: We hypothesize that S. agalactiae MprF and other MprF enzymes that utilize glycolipid substrates have unique patterns of interacting residues relative to those enzymes that use only PG as a substrate.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis by the authors.

claim: Important features of enzyme function like allostery or enzyme specificity may involve more than two residues.
source: While modeling how pairs of residues covary is powerful, many important features of enzyme function like allostery or enzyme specificity (which is the purpose of this analysis) may involve more than two residues (Goodey and Benkovic, 2008), and in these situations it can be difficult to connect sets of residues using solely pairwise parameters (Figliuzzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goodey and Benkovic, 2008 and Figliuzzi et al., 2018.

claim: Two positions (152 and 212) in the positive portion of the hidden unit correspond to residues 684 and 742, which were experimentally demonstrated to be relevant for aminoacylated-PG production.
source: Two positions in particular, 152 and 212, in the positive portion of the hidden unit correspond to residues 684 and 742, which were experimentally demonstrated to be relevant for aminoacylated-PG production by the Bacillus licheniformis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa cytosolic synthase domain variants (Hebecker et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hebecker et al., 2015.

claim: Full-length sequences included in the filtered dataset are enriched with sequences which contain the bacterial flippase domain.
source: We also note that the full-length sequences of the sequences included in our new dataset are enriched with sequences which contain the bacterial flippase domain (shown in red in Figure 4a), and the sequences we removed rarely contain the flippase domain (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for domain analysis).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: E. dispar synthesizes a novel cationic lipid, lysyl-diglucosyl(Glc2)-diacylglycerol (Lys-Glc2-DAG).
source: Remarkably, our lipidomic analysis found that E. dispar synthesizes a novel cationic lipid, lysyl-diglucosyl(Glc2)-diacylglycerol (Lys-Glc2-DAG) (Figure 1, Figure 6a and b), as well as Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results shown in Figures 1, 6a, 6b, 6c, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: E. dispar synthesizes Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG.
source: Remarkably, our lipidomic analysis found that E. dispar synthesizes a novel cationic lipid, lysyl-diglucosyl(Glc2)-diacylglycerol (Lys-Glc2-DAG) (Figure 1, Figure 6a and b), as well as Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results shown in Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structural identification of Lys-Glc-2-DAG was supported by exact mass measurement ([M+H]+ observed at m/z 1047.730; calculated m/z 1047.731) and tandem MS.
source: The structural identification of Lys-Glc-2-DAG was supported by exact mass measurement ([M+H]+ observed at m/z 1047.730; calculated m/z 1047.731) and tandem MS (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Lys-Glc2-DAG is highly retentive on a silica-based normal phase column and elutes off the column at the very end of the gradient.
source: Lys-Glc-2-DAG is unusually polar and charged for a lipid; chromatographically, Lys-Glc2-DAG is highly retentive on a silica-based normal phase column and elutes off the column at the very end of the gradient (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on chromatographic data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The use of an amino-based HPLC column led to much improved elution profiles for Lys-Glc2-DAG and other glyco- and lysine lipids.
source: The use of an amino-based HPLC column led to much improved elution profiles for Lys-Glc2-DAG and other glyco- and lysine lipids (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on chromatographic data shown in Figure 6.

claim: All Enterococcus strains examined were found to synthesize Lys-PG, Lys-Glc-DAG, and Lys-Glc2-DAG at varying levels.
source: All Enterococcus strains examined were found to synthesize Lys-PG, Lys-Glc-DAG, and Lys-Glc2-DAG at varying levels (Figure 7a and Table 2).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results shown in Figure 7a and Table 2.

claim: MprF-dependent Lys-PG production by E. faecalis and E. faecium was previously reported.
source: MprF-dependent Lys-PG production by E. faecalis and E. faecium was previously reported (Bao et al., 2012; Roy and Ibba, 2009), but cationic glycolipids production has not been previously reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2012 and Roy and Ibba, 2009.

claim: Cationic glycolipids production by E. faecalis and E. faecium has not been previously reported.
source: MprF-dependent Lys-PG production by E. faecalis and E. faecium was previously reported (Bao et al., 2012; Roy and Ibba, 2009), but cationic glycolipids production has not been previously reported.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the manuscript.

claim: E. gallinarium EG2 and E. casseliflavus EC10 encode a single copy of mprF gene.
source: E. gallinarium EG2 and E. casseliflavus EC10 encode a single copy of mprF gene, while the other enterococci we tested encode two distinct mprF genes (mprF1 and mprF2) (Bao et al., 2012; Roy and Ibba, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2012 and Roy and Ibba, 2009.

claim: Other enterococci tested encode two distinct mprF genes (mprF1 and mprF2).
source: E. gallinarium EG2 and E. casseliflavus EC10 encode a single copy of mprF gene, while the other enterococci we tested encode two distinct mprF genes (mprF1 and mprF2) (Bao et al., 2012; Roy and Ibba, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2012 and Roy and Ibba, 2009.

claim: Lys-PG, Lys-Glc-DAG, and Lys-Glc2-DAG were absent when the synthase domain of E. faecalis OG1RF_10760 mprF was disrupted.
source: lipidomic analysis on an E. faecalis OG1RF mini-mariner (EfaMarTn) transposon mutant (Dale et al., 2018) with a transposon insertion within OG1RF_10760 mprF (referred to as mprF2 in previous studies [Bao et al., 2012]; OG1RF_10760::Tn) revealed that Lys-PG, Lys-Glc-DAG, and the newly identified Lys-Glc2-DAG were absent when the synthase domain of the gene was disrupted (Figure 7b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis of a transposon mutant shown in Figure 7b.

claim: E. faecalis mprF2 is necessary for the synthesis of the three Lys-lipids in E. faecalis.
source: This led us to the conclusion that E. faecalis mprF2 is necessary for the synthesis of the three Lys-lipids in E. faecalis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transposon mutant analysis.

claim: Expression of E. faecalis mprF2 from a plasmid (pOGMprF2) complemented the phenotype of OG1RF_10760::Tn.
source: This phenotype was complemented by expression of E. faecalis mprF2 from a plasmid (pOGMprF2) (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is based on complementation experiment shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Expression of E. faecium mprF1 (EFTG_00601) (pEfMprF1) restored Lys-PG and Lys-Glc2-DAG synthesis to the E. faecalis OG1RF_10760::Tn strain.
source: Additionally, expression of E. faecium mprF1 (EFTG_00601) (pEfMprF1) restored Lys-PG and Lys-Glc2-DAG synthesis to the E. faecalis OG1RF_10760::Tn strain (Figure 7e), while E. faecium mprF2 (EFTG_02430) did not rescue Lys-lipid synthesis (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is based on complementation experiment shown in Figure 7e.

claim: E. faecium mprF2 (EFTG_02430) did not rescue Lys-lipid synthesis in E. faecalis OG1RF_10760::Tn strain.
source: Additionally, expression of E. faecium mprF1 (EFTG_00601) (pEfMprF1) restored Lys-PG and Lys-Glc2-DAG synthesis to the E. faecalis OG1RF_10760::Tn strain (Figure 7e), while E. faecium mprF2 (EFTG_02430) did not rescue Lys-lipid synthesis (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is based on complementation experiment shown in Figure 7f.

claim: E. faecalis MprF2 (OG1RF_10760) and E. faecium MprF1 (EFTG_00601) act on both phospholipid and glycolipids substrates.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that E. faecalis MprF2 (OG1RF_10760) and E. faecium MprF1 (EFTG_00601), like S. agalactiae MprF, act on both phospholipid and glycolipids substrates, additionally synthesizing the novel cationic glycolipid, Lys-Glc2-DAG.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation experiments.

claim: E. faecalis MprF2 (OG1RF_10760) and E. faecium MprF1 (EFTG_00601) synthesize the novel cationic glycolipid, Lys-Glc2-DAG.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that E. faecalis MprF2 (OG1RF_10760) and E. faecium MprF1 (EFTG_00601), like S. agalactiae MprF, act on both phospholipid and glycolipids substrates, additionally synthesizing the novel cationic glycolipid, Lys-Glc2-DAG.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation experiments.

claim: All strains tested synthesize Lys-PG.
source: All strains tested synthesize Lys-PG (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results shown in Table 2.

claim: Only L. brevis and L. paracasei synthesized Lys-Glc2-DAG among the Lactobacillus strains tested.
source: Only L. brevis and L. paracasei synthesized Lys-Glc2-DAG, L. paracasei synthesized low levels of Lys-Glc2-DAG.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results.

claim: L. paracasei synthesized low levels of Lys-Glc2-DAG.
source: Only L. brevis and L. paracasei synthesized Lys-Glc2-DAG, L. paracasei synthesized low levels of Lys-Glc2-DAG.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results.

claim: Exiguobacterium acetylicum UTDF19-27C was found to synthesize only Lys-PG.
source: An additional quadrant one (Q1) strain Exiguobacterium acetylicum UTDF19-27C was analyzed by lipidomics. It was found to synthesize only Lys-PG.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis results.

claim: Staphylococcus aureus RN4220 and Bacillus subtilis 168 synthesize only Lys-PG.
source: This MprF falls near Staphylococcus aureus RN4220 and Bacillus subtilis 168 in our plot, both of which synthesize only Lys-PG (Peschel et al., 2001; Slavetinsky et al., 2012) (and experimentally confirmed in this study).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peschel et al., 2001 and Slavetinsky et al., 2012, and experimentally confirmed in this study.

claim: Sequences which plot with positive activations in hidden unit 2 are more likely to have GlcN-DAG as a substrate (8/9).
source: With this plot, we can see that sequences which plot with positive activations in hidden unit 2 are more likely to have GlcN-DAG as a substrate (8/9), and sequences with negative values predominantly use PG (7/11), with a Fisher's exact test p-value of 0.028 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental results with a Fisher's exact test p-value of 0.028.

claim: Sequences with negative values in hidden unit 2 predominantly use PG (7/11).
source: With this plot, we can see that sequences which plot with positive activations in hidden unit 2 are more likely to have GlcN-DAG as a substrate (8/9), and sequences with negative values predominantly use PG (7/11), with a Fisher's exact test p-value of 0.028 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental results with a Fisher's exact test p-value of 0.028.

claim: Hidden unit 2 is correlated with GlcN-DAG specificity with a Fisher's exact test p-value of 0.028.
source: With this plot, we can see that sequences which plot with positive activations in hidden unit 2 are more likely to have GlcN-DAG as a substrate (8/9), and sequences with negative values predominantly use PG (7/11), with a Fisher's exact test p-value of 0.028 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental results.

claim: Hidden unit 1 is not correlated with GlcN-DAG specificity, with a Fisher's exact p-value of 0.67.
source: Hidden unit 1, however, is not correlated with GlcN-DAG specificity, with a Fisher's exact p-value of 0.67.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental results.

claim: Hidden unit 2, and thus the high magnitude sequence positions identified by it, are correlated with GlcN-DAG specificity.
source: Therefore, we conclude that hidden unit 2, and thus the high magnitude sequence positions identified by it, are correlated with GlcN-DAG specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the statistical analysis.

claim: BLASTp did not identify other streptococcal MprFs capable of lysine addition to both glycolipid and phospholipid substrates.
source: Importantly, although highly similar to S. agalactiae MprF, this method did not identify other streptococcal MprFs capable of lysine addition to both glycolipid and phospholipid substrates (generating Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG) nor did it lead to the identification of a novel cationic glycolipid found in Enterococcus.
evidence: This is a limitation of the BLASTp method as discussed by the authors.

claim: BLASTp did not lead to the identification of a novel cationic glycolipid found in Enterococcus.
source: Importantly, although highly similar to S. agalactiae MprF, this method did not identify other streptococcal MprFs capable of lysine addition to both glycolipid and phospholipid substrates (generating Lys-Glc-DAG and Lys-PG) nor did it lead to the identification of a novel cationic glycolipid found in Enterococcus.
evidence: This is a limitation of the BLASTp method as discussed by the authors.

claim: Methods which model the strength of amino acid coevolution in sequence sets can find important signals which in the sequence logo might appear to be negligible.
source: When amino acids must interact to produce a specific function, yet the exact identity of those amino acids is not a requirement, methods which model the strength of amino acid coevolution in sequence sets can find important signals which in the sequence logo might appear to be negligible.
evidence: This is a rationale for using the RBM method.

claim: The two hidden units which formed the basis of the specificity analysis were not found in models trained on the Pfam dataset when it was initially pulled from Pfam.
source: First, it allowed us to filter the sequence data using hidden units (Figure 4); the two hidden units which formed the basis of our specificity analysis were not found in models trained on the Pfam dataset when it was initially pulled from Pfam, and this was potentially due to the presence of sequences without relevant catalytic function adding noise to the dataset.
evidence: This is an observation about the model training process.

claim: The presence of sequences without relevant catalytic function potentially added noise to the initial Pfam dataset.
source: First, it allowed us to filter the sequence data using hidden units (Figure 4); the two hidden units which formed the basis of our specificity analysis were not found in models trained on the Pfam dataset when it was initially pulled from Pfam, and this was potentially due to the presence of sequences without relevant catalytic function adding noise to the dataset.
evidence: This is a speculation about why the hidden units were not found in the initial model.

claim: The E. faecium allele EGTF_00601 has sequence features placing it in quadrant one yet has GlcN-DAG activity.
source: However, there are notable exceptions such as the E. faecium allele EGTF_00601, which has sequence features placing it in quadrant one yet has GlcN-DAG activity.
evidence: This is an observation about an exception to the general pattern.

claim: Identifying the exact sequence determinants of GlcN-DAG specificity remains to be fully elucidated.
source: Therefore, identifying the exact sequence determinants of GlcN-DAG specificity remains to be fully elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: Important residue interactions determining specificity could occur in the N-terminal flippase domain and the non-cytosolic region of the C-terminal domain.
source: One explanation could be our exclusion of the N-terminal flippase domain and the non-cytosolic region of the C-terminal domain in the RBM analysis, where important residue interactions determining specificity could occur and is under further investigation.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential explanations for the incomplete understanding of specificity determinants.

claim: Lipids produced may vary during the growth phase of the organisms, the media they are grown in, and whether a membrane stressor is present.
source: When using native organisms, lipids produced may vary during the growth phase of the organisms, the media they are grown in, and whether a membrane stressor is present (i.e. inducible production of specific lipids).
evidence: This is a discussion of experimental challenges.

claim: The use of a heterologous host for expression of mprF alleles may result in not identifying novel lipids that would be found in their native bacteria since the appropriate lipid substrates may not be present.
source: The use of a heterologous host for expression of mprF alleles is a method of standardization, but may result in not identifying novel lipids that would be found in their native bacteria since the appropriate lipid substrates may not be present (Joyce et al., 2019; Joyce et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joyce et al., 2019 and Joyce et al., 2021.

claim: The residues identified through hidden units can be thought of as templates for mutational exploration, greatly reducing the search space for assessing which residues are critical for specificity determination.
source: Concretely, the residues identified through hidden units can be thought of as templates for mutational exploration, greatly reducing the search space for assessing which residues are critical for specificity determination.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential applications of the RBM method.

claim: Enzymes like MprF that produce lipids of modified charge have potential applications in biotechnology and therapeutics.
source: Enzymes like MprF that produce lipids of modified charge have potential applications in biotechnology and therapeutics, where the design of lipid nanoparticles with different charge and chemical properties of the head group have important physiological implications (Carrasco et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carrasco et al., 2021.

claim: The identification of Lys-Glc2-DAG opens new research avenues, particularly in the fields of antibiotic resistance and host-pathogen interactions.
source: Notably, the identification of Lys-Glc2-DAG opens new research avenues, particularly in the fields of antibiotic resistance and host-pathogen interactions, wherein lipid modification and cationic lipids play key roles.
evidence: This is a discussion of the implications of the findings.

claim: It would be relevant to investigate whether Lys-Glc2-DAG plays a role in enterococcal resistance to daptomycin.
source: With respect to human health, it would be relevant to investigate whether Lys-Glc2-DAG plays a role in enterococcal resistance to the last-line membrane-active antibiotic, daptomycin.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.
